Question: Whether frustrated desire resulting from the loss of a desired object is greater than that from failure to obtain a desired object?
Notes: For instance, is it more stressful to be in a friendship with somone, only for that friendship to end (e.g., death, travel, a falling out) or to desire a friendship, but be unable to obtain it (e.g., no suitable person, or not being accepted by another). The relevance is that on the current doctrine of desire to which I am sympathetic, the act of desire and craving, on the right senses of those words, is itself stressful (rooted in dissatisfaction). The stress and suffering that "results" from frustrated desire (e.g., wanting something and not getting it) is simply the revelation or the uncovering of the stress inherent in that desire, which is, otherwise, say, suppressed by one's indulgence in the object thereof. For instance, imagine someone who takes a medication for psoriasis that allays any symptoms of itching. Suppose one week they travel abroad. They didn't realize they needed a refill and they left with only enough medication for a day, and are without means to refill it on their travels. As a result, in some sense of the word, they experience intense itching. In fact, though, the lack of medication (the frustrated desire here) does not cause the itching. The psoriasis does and the medication simply suppresses it. This is roughly analogous to the doctrine of desire and craving I am sympathetic to. The craving is the psoriasis, the resulting dissatisfaction, which could very well just be called an itch of the mind, is the itch, and the objects of ones craving, often sensual pleasures, are the medicine (the analogy breaks down here, as on this doctrine, indulgence in desired objects exacerbates the craving, the disease, and so is not exactly medicine; to the extent of its alleviating effect though, the fact that it worsens the disease notwithstanding, it is like medicine). In any case, it might seem to some that the frustration of a desire resulting from loss of an obtained object is worse than that from the failure to gain an unobtained object. I thought of this when I recalled that I was told by a professional psychiatrist that patients often rate heartbreak as the greatest pain (or something like that), and I considered if this has any relevance or is a challenge to the aforementioned doctrine.
